Forecast types

Five steps

At each step: first physics, then what AI changes.

Step 1

Observe

Measurements

Station
Radiosonde
Radar
Satellites

Photos: radiosonde and satellite image NOAA, public domain; radar The Bushranger, CC BY-SA 4.0. Station map: WMO

Step 2

Analyse

Analysis

Recent observations and the previous forecast are combined into one complete map of the atmosphere now. This is data assimilation.

Step 3

Simulate

Physics models

The model splits the atmosphere into boxes. In each box it solves the equations of motion, heat and moisture, step by step.

9 km

IFS, the physics model of ECMWF (the European weather centre): 137 levels, a time step of a few minutes.

Boxes exchange air, heat and water with their neighbours, sideways and up and down.

Model components

One forecast is several models running together: atmosphere, ocean waves, ocean and sea ice.

They exchange heat, water and wind stress every time step or every hour.

ECMWF IFS, cycle 49r1 (from autumn 2024). Source: ECMWF

Resolution

Anything smaller than a box, a thunderstorm for example, is described by simplified rules (parametrisation).

Resolution of the AI model

ECMWF's AI model, AIFS (more on it soon), has a 30 km grid instead of 9 km. Mountains get lower; narrow valleys and bays disappear.

Surface height on the AIFS grid. ECMWF open data

Forecast quality

1 °C

typical temperature error on the first day

2.5 °C

after a week

The atmosphere is chaotic: small errors in the starting map grow, and one forecast cannot show how much.

Mean absolute error of 2 m temperature by lead time (hours). Coloured lines: individual forecast dates; black: their mean. Source: Meteoblue

Ensembles

ECMWF runs 51 slightly different forecasts, called ensemble members. Their spread shows the uncertainty.

Image: Met Office

The AI approach

→
…
…

Trained on 40+ years of weather, the network draws the maps 6 hours ahead; each output becomes the next input, like video frames. 15 days take about a minute.

Our example: AIFS, in daily use at ECMWF since 2025. Top: AIFS input and output fields. Bottom: temperature at about 1.5 km and sea-level pressure. AIFS forecast from 16 November 2026, 00 UTC, ECMWF open data

Learning

Each dot is a past day. The line is the pattern. It gives a good guess for a day it has never seen.

The dashed curve hits every past day but misses the new one: it memorised the examples instead of finding the pattern.

A neural network does the same with millions to billions of adjustable numbers instead of two (slope and offset).

Training

→
vs
=

The network nudges its numbers to reduce the error, then moves on to the next examples. AIFS made 260,000 such adjustments on ERA5, past weather from 1979 to 2022.

Error: red where the guess was too warm, blue where too cold, up to 3 °C. Real AIFS forecast and analysis, 16 November 2026. In training, "what happened" comes from ERA5.

AIFS vs physics

How closely the forecast map matches reality; 100% is perfect.

Red: physics model IFS.
Blue: AI model AIFS.

ECMWF reports gains of up to 20%, for example for tropical cyclone tracks.

Blurring and ensembles

A network trained to be right on average draws the smooth average and washes storms out. A generative model adds random numbers to each run, so every forecast stays sharp.

AIFS ensemble, forecast for 1 December 2026 made on 16 November. ECMWF open data

Physics vs AI

Physics modelAI model
How it worksEquations of physics on a gridPatterns learned from 40+ years of past weather
Starting pointAnalysis of observationsThe same physics analysis
Forecast runA supercomputerAbout a minute on one GPU, ~1,000× less energy
Grid9 km (ECMWF IFS)About 30 km (AIFS)
Large-scale weatherReferenceMore accurate on most scores
Ensemble51 members, expensiveCheap; Google's GenCast beat ECMWF's on 97% of scores
Record extremes, small stormsBetter, within grid limitsOften too weak or missing

Sources: ECMWF; Price et al., 2024 (GenCast)

Limitations

  • Storms stronger than anything in the training data
  • Tropical cyclones: tracks better, peak strength worse
  • Thunderstorms like this one: smaller than a 30 km grid box
  • They need the physics analysis: when ECMWF changed it in 2026, several AI models, including an older AIFS, got worse.

Supercell at sunset. Photo via Nevreme Srbija (t.me/nenevreme)

Nowcasting

A weather radar shows where it rains and how hard, up to about 200 km away, every 5 minutes.

A global physics forecast arrives hours after its start time. Nowcasting uses the latest radar pictures for the next few hours.

Where will the rain be in an hour?

Pictures 20 minutes apart, 17 November 2026, 19:30 to 21:10 UTC. RainViewer radar composite

How a nowcast works

The same recipe as AIFS, on radar pictures: the last hour in, the next hour out.

Classical extrapolation only moves the rain along. A network trained on years of radar also learns how showers grow and decay.

Radar over the Balkans, 17 November 2026, pictures 20 minutes apart (RainViewer). Right: what actually happened, the target the network learns to reproduce.

Nowcast vs model

Extrapolation is best for the first hours, then the physics model takes over. AI nowcasts keep the lead much longer.

Schematic. Published crossovers: radar extrapolation vs a 3 km physics model at 3–6 h; MetNet-3 (Google, 2023) vs physics models at 15–24 h, depending on rain intensity.

Step 4

Correct

Post-processing

Compare each model's past forecasts with what stations measured, learn the typical errors, and correct the new forecast.

Statistics since 1972 (Model Output Statistics); today machine learning, for each station, season and weather type.

Step 5

Deliver

Delivery

From observations to your app, for a run started at 00 UTC. Global and regional models take hours, so the forecast reaches apps after 06 UTC.

Delivery with AI

The analysis is still physics and takes as long. The AI model replaces the global and regional runs and takes minutes, so the forecast reaches apps earlier.

Who builds AI weather models

Weather services

  • ECMWF: AIFS
  • NOAA (USA): AIGFS
  • DWD (Germany): AICON
  • Met Office (UK), MET Norway, MeteoSwiss

Cheaper, faster forecasts and bigger ensembles, next to physics models

Big tech

  • Google: GenCast, WeatherNext
  • Microsoft: Aurora
  • NVIDIA: Earth-2
  • Huawei: Pangu-Weather

Forecasts for their products; cloud and GPUs to sell

Chinese labs

  • Shanghai AI Lab: FengWu
  • Fudan University: FuXi
  • Tsinghua and China's weather service: NowcastNet

Research for the national weather service, tools for export

Startups

  • WindBorne: balloons + AI
  • Jua: energy trading
  • Silurian
  • Brightband

Forecasts sold to energy, insurance and defence

Serbia has been an ECMWF member since 2015: RHMZ gets AIFS forecasts directly.

Sources: ECMWF; NOAA (Dec 2025); DWD (Mar 2026); company announcements, 2024–2026

Who uses forecasts

Faster and cheaper forecasts make new uses affordable.

EnergyWind and solar output, grid balance, power trading
InsuranceDamage risk from storms, floods and hail
TransportFlight delays, ship routes, road conditions
AgricultureFrost, hail, drought, when to irrigate
LogisticsStore demand, supply disruptions
Public safetyWarnings for floods and storms

Weather forecasting services: about $3 bn a year and growing; energy and renewables are the fastest-growing buyers. Market reports, 2025; estimates vary.

Where geographers come in

AI is weakest where geography shapes the weather.

  • TerrainMountains, coasts and cities are blurred on a 30 km grid.
  • Local effectsKošava gusts, valley fog, urban heat: shaped by terrain and land cover.
  • DownscalingAI sharpens coarse forecasts using relief and land-cover maps.
  • ImpactWhat the rain means for a river basin, a field or a city.

Summary

  • A forecast is a chain: observe, analyse, simulate, correct, deliver.
  • An AI model learns a 6-hour step from 40 years of past weather and repeats it.
  • It takes about a minute on one GPU and is more accurate for large-scale weather.
  • It still starts from a physics analysis and learns from physics-made data.
  • Weak spots: rare extremes, small storms, mountains and coasts.
